content: 1. Before initiating the procedure, ensure that all necessary equipment is prepared and ready for use. 2. Position the child either on their back or side. An assistant should be present to help hold the child securely during the procedure. 3. Measure the distance from the child’s nose to their stomach to estimate the length of the nasogastric tube that needs to be inserted to reach the stomach. 4. Attach a syringe to the nasogastric tube. 5. Carefully and gently insert the nasogastric tube through the child’s nose and advance it into the stomach. 6. Using the syringe attached to the nasogastric tube, aspirate 2–5 mL of gastric contents. 7. To confirm the correct placement of the tube, test the aspirated gastric contents with litmus paper. Blue litmus paper should turn red in response to the acidic stomach contents. Alternatively, inject 3–5 mL of air into the stomach through the tube and listen for a sound over the stomach using a stethoscope. 8. If no fluid is aspirated, inject 5–10 mL of sterile water or normal saline into the tube and attempt to aspirate again. If still unsuccessful, repeat the procedure. Note that even if the tube is incorrectly positioned and water or saline enters the airways, the risk of adverse events is minimal. Do not repeat the procedure more than three times. 9. Once gastric contents are successfully aspirated, aim to collect at least 5–10 mL. 10. Transfer the aspirated gastric fluid from the syringe into a sterile container, such as a sputum collection cup. 11. Add an equal volume of sodium bicarbonate solution to the specimen to neutralize the acidic gastric contents and prevent destruction of tubercle bacilli. After the procedure: 1. Wipe the exterior of the specimen container with alcohol or chlorhexidine to prevent cross-infection, and label the container appropriately. 2. Complete the necessary laboratory requisition forms. 3. Transport the specimen to the laboratory for processing as soon as possible, ideally within 4 hours, using a cool box. 4. If transportation is expected to take longer than 4 hours, store the specimen in a refrigerator at 4–8°C until it can be transported. 5. Allow the child to resume their usual diet. Safety considerations: Gastric aspiration is generally not an aerosol-generating procedure. Young children are at low risk of transmitting infections, making gastric aspiration a low-risk procedure for tuberculosis (TB) transmission. It can be safely performed at the child’s bedside or in a routine procedure room. Sputum induction: Unlike gastric aspiration, sputum induction is an aerosol-generating procedure. Whenever possible, perform this procedure in an isolation room equipped with adequate infection control measures, such as negative pressure, ultraviolet light (used when the room is unoccupied), and an extractor fan. Sputum induction is considered a low-risk procedure for the child being evaluated for TB. Adverse events are rare but may include coughing spells, mild wheezing, and nosebleeds. Recent studies indicate that sputum induction can be safely performed even in young infants, provided that staff are adequately trained and equipped. Pre-procedure considerations: Assess the child beforehand to ensure they are well enough to undergo the procedure. Children with the following conditions should not undergo sputum induction: Inadequate fasting (less than 3 hours); Severe respiratory distress (e.g., rapid breathing, wheezing, hypoxia); Intubation; Bleeding disorders (e.g., low platelet count, bleeding tendency, severe nosebleeds); Reduced level of consciousness; History of significant asthma diagnosed and treated by a clinician. Sputum induction procedure: 1. Administer a bronchodilator (e.g., salbutamol) to reduce the risk of wheezing. 2. Administer nebulized hypertonic saline (3% NaCl) for 15 minutes or until 5 mL of solution has been fully delivered. 3. Perform chest physiotherapy if necessary to mobilize secretions. 4. For older children capable of expectorating, follow the procedures outlined under “Expectoration” to collect sputum. 5. For younger children unable to expectorate, perform either: Suctioning of the nasal passages to remove nasal secretions; or Nasopharyngeal aspiration to collect an adequate specimen. Equipment considerations: Any equipment intended for reuse must be thoroughly disinfected and sterilized before being used on another patient. References: 1. Laboratory services in tuberculosis control. 2. Zar HJ et al. Sputum induction for the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis in infants and young children in an urban setting in South Africa. Archives of Disease in Childhood, 2000, 82:305–308. Dosing guidelines for anti-TB drugs in children: Use quality-assured dispersible tablets whenever possible, especially for children who cannot swallow solid tablets. Regimens are based on fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) but may require additional single-component products in some cases. Doses are designed for once-daily administration and aim to avoid splitting tablets. Recommended doses are generally below the upper limit of the dose range to minimize toxicity risks. Once children reach a body weight of 25 kg, adult dosage recommendations and preparations can be used.
